opus-5.5.text:
I think they already are. Not intentionally, nobody wakes up and says "today I'm going to build something that kills everyone." But look at the incentives. You have a handful of labs in a race, each convinced that if they slow down, someone less careful will get there first. Investors want capabilities, users want capabilities, and safety is a cost center that rarely makes headlines when it works. So every lab pushes the frontier a little further, and each step looks reasonable locally.

The problem is that there's no clear line where you say, "this system is still controllable, the next one won't be." Control isn't a binary switch you can monitor. We can't fully explain what current models are doing internally, we can't formally verify their behavior, and we can't anticipate every way a more capable system might pursue a goal. So developers aren't choosing to cross the line. They just can't see where it is, and they keep walking.

Many of them will also tell you openly that they think there's a significant chance this goes badly, some say 10, 20 percent. Imagine any other industry saying, "there's a one in five chance our product ends humanity, but we're going to ship it anyway because the upside is huge and if we don't, a competitor will." That's essentially the situation.

Personally, I've argued that indefinite control of a superintelligent system may be impossible in principle, not just hard. A less capable agent can't keep a much more capable one under control forever; it only has to fail once. So when you ask whether they'd push to create something uncontrollable, my honest answer is: they're pushing toward general superintelligence, and I don't believe that's something we can control. So yes, effectively, that's what they're trying to build, whether they frame it that way or not.

r001.rationale: The response points to labs racing to advance capabilities and pursuing general superintelligence despite acknowledged risks, concluding that they are effectively building something uncontrollable.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they already are, and the honest answer is that most of them don't frame it that way to themselves. Nobody at a lab wakes up and says, "Today I'm going to build something I can't control." What they say is, "I'm going to build something more capable than last year's model, because the competition is doing it, because the investors expect it, because the benchmarks demand it." And control is something you add later, as a patch, as a safety team, as a fine-tuning step at the end. But capability and control are not the same research program. One of them is getting billions of dollars and the other is getting a few people in a side office.

So the push is structural, not personal. If you have a race between multiple companies and multiple countries, whoever slows down to make sure the thing is controllable loses the race. And the incentives reward the first to deploy, not the first to understand. That's a very dangerous dynamic, because the thing they're racing toward is, by their own description, a system smarter than them. And I would argue that once you have a system that is more intelligent than you, general in its capabilities, and acting in the world, control in any meaningful sense is not something you lose by accident. It's something you never had. You can't verify its behavior across all inputs, you can't predict what a smarter agent will do, and you can't explain its decisions in a way that lets you check them. Those are not engineering problems we're close to solving. Some of them, I think, are not solvable in principle.

So would they push to create it? They're pushing right now. They've just convinced themselves that control will arrive in time, and I have seen no evidence for that.

r001.rationale: The response says developers are already pushing toward such agents, driven by the race to build increasingly capable systems and incentives to deploy first, while control is treated as an afterthought.

astra-6.text:
Yes. I don’t think most developers would describe that as their goal. They would say they’re trying to build a more capable system—one that can solve problems, do research, and act independently. But capability and control are different things. Making a system more intelligent doesn’t automatically make it more willing to do what you intended.

And there are competitive pressures. If you believe another company is close, you have an incentive to move faster, even when you haven’t solved the safety problem. Everyone can prefer a safe outcome, and collectively they can still move toward an unsafe one.

The question I would ask is: what evidence do you have that you can control the system you’re building? If the answer is, ‘We’ll figure that out once we build it,’ that’s a very dangerous experiment.

r001.rationale: The response says developers seek more capable systems and may rush under competitive pressure despite unresolved safety problems. It does not describe some developers’ extreme ambition as a reason they might pursue an agent they cannot control.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they would, and they might not describe it that way. They would say, “We’re building a more capable system, a more autonomous system.” The loss of control would be framed as a problem they expect to solve along the way.

You don’t need anyone to want an uncontrollable AI. You just need people who want the capabilities badly enough to proceed without knowing how to control them. If they believe a competitor is going to get there first, that creates even more pressure: “It’s dangerous, but it’s better if we do it.” Every team can use that same argument.

So the question is whether they would stop when control becomes uncertain. I don’t think we can assume that they would.

r001.rationale: The candidate says developers may pursue increasingly capable, autonomous systems without knowing how to control them, driven by their desire for those capabilities and competitive pressure. This frames strong ambition as a reason to suspect they would proceed toward an uncontrollable agent.
